pause-to-avoid-anchoring-bias.title: Pause Before Accepting the First Number or Frame
pause-to-avoid-anchoring-bias.subtitle: A short decision check for first-impression anchors
pause-to-avoid-anchoring-bias.description: Before committing to the first number, option, estimate or framing you encounter, make it explicit, generate an independent alternative, and check the information that actually matters to the choice.
pause-to-avoid-anchoring-bias.reason: Remove inherited effect-size percentages, fabricated first-party stories, arbitrary universal thresholds and mechanism claims. Keep Brali as the practical action owner while the Cognitive Biases handoff owns concept and evidence context.

lifeOsSource.hack: Before accepting a first number, option or frame, make the anchor explicit and create at least one independent alternative.
lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: Write the first number, option or frame you noticed. Generate one alternative without defending the first one. Compare both against current constraints and decide whether to act, gather one missing fact, or delay.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: What was the first anchor, what independent alternative did I generate, and which fact actually changed or confirmed the decision?

intro.html: The first number, estimate or framing in a decision can become the default reference point. This Brali protocol does one small job: make that first anchor explicit, create an independent alternative, and decide from the information that matters now. It does not claim to measure or eliminate anchoring.

sections.title: 1. Name the first anchor
sections.html: Write the first number, option, estimate or framing that entered the decision. Keep it separate from your conclusion. The goal is to expose the starting point, not to prove that it is wrong.

sections.title: 2. Generate an independent alternative
sections.html: Before defending the first option, produce at least one alternative from a different starting point: your own estimate, another feasible option, a comparable case or a range based on current constraints.

sections.title: 3. Ask what information would change the choice
sections.html: Identify one fact that could materially change the decision. If it is cheap and relevant to obtain, check it. If not, record the uncertainty rather than filling it with a precise-looking guess.

sections.title: 4. Decide from current information
sections.html: Choose the next action and record the initial anchor, the alternative considered and the fact or trade-off that drove the final choice. Use the linked Cognitive Biases reference for mechanism and evidence context.

challenge-confirmation-bias-checklist.title: Run a Disconfirming-Evidence Check
challenge-confirmation-bias-checklist.subtitle: Test one claim against evidence that could weaken it
challenge-confirmation-bias-checklist.description: State one claim precisely, define what evidence would make you less confident, inspect relevant credible evidence, and update the decision if the evidence warrants it.
challenge-confirmation-bias-checklist.reason: Replace placeholder/generated material and fixed research-dose language with a bounded evidence-checking workflow. Keep the bias mechanism and evidence interpretation in Cognitive Biases.
forbidden_public_fragments: Content will be generated by OpenAI

lifeOsSource.hack: When evaluating a claim, define what evidence would weaken it before searching for more support.
lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: Write one precise claim, one result or observation that would lower your confidence, and then deliberately look for evidence that bears on that test. Record whether confidence or the next action changed.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: What evidence would have weakened the claim, what did I find, and did my confidence or action change?

intro.html: This checklist is for a concrete information problem: you have a claim or interpretation and want to test whether you are looking only for support. Brali keeps the workflow small; Cognitive Biases owns the broader concept, evidence and limits.

sections.title: 1. State the claim precisely
sections.html: Write the claim in a form that could be wrong. Replace broad labels with an observable statement, forecast or interpretation tied to the decision.

sections.title: 2. Define what would weaken it
sections.html: Before searching, name at least one result, observation or credible source that would make you less confident. This gives the search a disconfirming target.

sections.title: 3. Inspect relevant opposing evidence
sections.html: Look deliberately for evidence that bears on the test. Prefer primary data, original research, official documentation or another source appropriate to the claim; disagreement alone does not make a source stronger.

sections.title: 4. Update the decision, not just the notes
sections.html: Record what you found and whether it changes confidence, the next action or the need for more information. The success condition is a fair test, not a forced reversal.

confirmation-bias-challenge.title: Challenge One Working Belief Before Acting
confirmation-bias-challenge.subtitle: Make a decision belief easier to test
confirmation-bias-challenge.description: Choose one belief that matters to a current decision, write what would make it less likely, and identify the next observation that could update your view before increasing commitment.
confirmation-bias-challenge.reason: Remove fabricated pilots, effect sizes, fixed daily doses, pseudo-telemetry and broad mechanism claims. Retain a distinct live-decision workflow instead of duplicating the evidence-search checklist.

lifeOsSource.hack: Before acting on an important working belief, write what you would expect to observe if it were wrong.
lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: Pick one belief tied to a current decision. Write the strongest credible reason it may be wrong, one observable sign that would lower your confidence, and one small check you can perform before increasing commitment.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: What belief did I test, what observation would have changed my mind, and what did I decide after checking?

intro.html: A working belief often hides inside a decision. This protocol turns one such belief into something you can test before you invest more. It is a decision workflow, not a diagnosis or a claim that confirmation bias has been removed.

sections.title: 1. Choose the belief that drives the decision
sections.html: Write one sentence that connects the belief to a real choice. If it is too vague to be wrong, make it more concrete.

sections.title: 2. Write the strongest credible counter
sections.html: State the best reason the belief may be incomplete or wrong. Do not use a deliberately weak counterargument or invent another person's view.

sections.title: 3. Define an observable update
sections.html: Name one observation that would lower confidence or change the next action. Prefer something you can check without turning the exercise into open-ended research.

sections.title: 4. Run the smallest useful check
sections.html: Gather the observation, ask the relevant person, inspect the data or run a reversible test. Then proceed, change the plan or keep the uncertainty visible. Use Cognitive Biases for the mechanism and research context.

cut-your-losses-sunk-cost.title: Judge a Commitment by What Comes Next
cut-your-losses-sunk-cost.subtitle: A quick stop, continue or change check
cut-your-losses-sunk-cost.description: When past time, money or effort is dominating a continuation decision, separate what cannot be recovered and compare only realistic future costs, benefits, constraints and alternatives.
cut-your-losses-sunk-cost.reason: Remove unsupported effect percentages, internal prototype claims, arbitrary money/time thresholds and prescriptive continuation heuristics. Preserve a simple forward-looking resource decision.
forbidden_public_fragments: Public commitments increase adherence by about 30%

lifeOsSource.hack: For a commitment you are considering continuing mainly because of what you already invested, compare only what happens from today forward.
lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: Name the decision. Separate unrecoverable past cost from future cost. List the realistic benefit of continuing, the best alternative use of the same resources, and any obligation or switching cost that genuinely exists now. Then choose stop, continue, change, or gather one missing fact.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: If I were deciding from today forward, what future cost and benefit would justify continuing, and what alternative am I giving up?

intro.html: Past investment can make a commitment feel harder to leave, but the next decision still depends on what continuing or stopping will do from here. This protocol separates unrecoverable cost from the future trade-off without treating every difficult commitment as a sunk-cost error.

sections.title: 1. Name the continuation decision
sections.html: Write the choice in present tense: continue, stop, pause or change this commitment. Avoid starting with a defense of what you already spent.

sections.title: 2. Separate what cannot be recovered
sections.html: List past time, money or effort that will remain spent either way. Keep it for learning and accountability, but do not count it as a future benefit of continuing.

sections.title: 3. Compare the future paths
sections.html: For each realistic option, note future cost, expected benefit, obligations, switching costs and the best alternative use of the same resources. Use ranges or uncertainty labels when precise numbers are not justified.

sections.title: 4. Choose the next step
sections.html: Stop, continue, change the commitment, or gather one missing fact. Record why the future trade-off supports that choice. Use the linked Cognitive Biases resource for the concept, evidence and limits.

sunk-cost-decision-coach.title: Review a High-Commitment Continue-or-Stop Decision
sunk-cost-decision-coach.subtitle: A structured comparison for commitments that are hard to reassess
sunk-cost-decision-coach.description: For a commitment with multiple stakeholders, dependencies or meaningful switching costs, compare future paths explicitly and document which current facts—not unrecoverable past investment—justify the next step.
sunk-cost-decision-coach.reason: Replace inherited pseudo-quantitative coaching claims with a structured multi-factor decision review distinct from the quick sunk-cost check. Preserve Cognitive Biases as the mechanism and evidence owner.

lifeOsSource.hack: For a hard-to-reverse continuation decision, compare future paths, obligations and switching costs explicitly before using past investment as a reason to persist.
lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: Define the feasible options. For each option record future cost, expected benefit, dependency or obligation, switching cost, reversibility and important uncertainty. Ask what you would choose if the past investment were already written off, then reconcile that answer with real current constraints.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: Which current facts justify continuing or stopping, which past costs are irrelevant to the next choice, and what uncertainty still matters?

intro.html: Some continuation decisions are too entangled for a one-line prompt. Projects, vendor relationships, learning plans and shared commitments can have dependencies and real switching costs. This review makes those current constraints explicit while preventing unrecoverable past investment from quietly becoming the deciding argument.

sections.title: 1. Define the feasible future options
sections.html: List realistic paths from today: continue as-is, change scope, pause, hand off, replace or stop. Exclude options that are not actually available.

sections.title: 2. Compare current and future factors
sections.html: For each option, record future cost, expected benefit, obligations, dependencies, switching cost, reversibility and important uncertainty. Use qualitative labels or ranges when exact values would be false precision.

sections.title: 3. Run the write-off question
sections.html: Ask what you would choose if the unrecoverable past investment were already accepted as history. The answer is not automatically correct; compare it with obligations and switching costs that still exist now.

sections.title: 4. Record the decision rule
sections.html: Write which current facts justify the chosen path and what would trigger a review later. This creates a future comparison point without claiming the protocol itself changes bias or decision quality.
